Listen to this article Share As global political attention focuses on major power dynamics, a key democratic contest on the Caribbean island state of Grenada on November 5, 2026, carries a surprisingly direct connection to Nigeria. Prime Minister Dickon Mitchell’s governing National Democratic Congress (NDC), which won nine of 15 parliamentary seats in 2022, faces a re-election challenge from the New National Party (NNP), led by Emmalin Pierre, and the Democratic People’s Movement (DPM), founded by former foreign minister Peter David. In a tri-island nation of under 130,000 residents, Nigerian development finance, private industrialists, state governors, and passport buyers have emerged as central topics in domestic campaign arguments. Project Polaris and the Stalled Development Finance Promise At the heart of the campaign is Project Polaris, a $250 million planned medical city in Hope Vale anchored by a 250-bed climate-resilient smart hospital designed with advisory support from New York’s Mount Sinai Health System. Groundbreaking occurred after the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), under Benedict Oramah, a Nigerian who led the bank for a decade, pledged co-financing as part of a broader $3 billion regional allocation for Caribbean development. However, as polling day approaches, the project remains incomplete. While the government has secured $185 million, including a $30 million contribution from the OPEC Fund, talks with Afreximbank stalled over contractual conditions. Bilateral diplomacy: From Lekki to Jalingo Mitchell’s political strategy has featured visible ties with Nigerian power brokers. In October 2024, Mitchell toured the Dangote refinery complex in Lekki alongside Aliko Dangote and Babajide Sanwo-Olu, Lagos State governor. Dangote subsequently visited St. George’s for Grenada’s 51st independence celebrations, donating 1,000 cricket kits to Mitchell’s constituency. Mitchell also established sub-national links with Agbu Kefas, Taraba State governor, attending the Nwonyo Fishing Festival in Ibi in April, before Kefas sponsored over 220 performers to Grenada’s African Liberation Festival. These high-profile relationships have sparked local debate; in the absence of campaign finance disclosure laws, unsubstantiated rumors regarding foreign campaign contributions have circulated across the island. Passport economy and diplomatic scrutiny The most lucrative link involves Grenada’s Citizenship-by-Investment (CBI) program. Starting at a $235,000 contribution to the National Transformation Fund, the program attracts wealthy Nigerians seeking visa-free access to the Schengen zone and eligibility for the United States E-2 treaty investor visa. Yet, this revenue stream faces impending regulatory hurdles. The European Commission has requested that Caribbean CBI countries phase out investor citizenship by June 1, 2028, while the United States has placed Grenada on a visitor visa bond list. Remarkably, this transatlantic connection exists without a formal foreign policy strategy from Abuja. When President Bola Tinubu visited the Caribbean, his official state visit targeted Saint Lucia before attending the BRICS summit in Brazil. Instead, Grenada’s campaign underscores how private capital, regional bankers, and state governors have constructed an informal foreign policy whose political viability will be tested when Grenadian voters cast their ballots.
